props.title: Thursday

sections.content: **Thursday** (1998) marked a pivotal moment in post-Tarantino crime cinema, following a reformed criminal through one chaotic day. Like **Pulp Fiction** (1994) and **The Way of the Gun** (2000), it plays with nonlinear storytelling and dark humor, but adds a distinct suburban anxiety. Director Skip Woods crafts a pressure-cooker narrative that owes clear debts to **True Romance** (1993) and **Things to Do in Denver When You're Dead** (1995), while carving its own niche in the crime genre.

sections.content: The late 90s saw a wave of complex crime narratives exploring the collision of suburban life with criminal underworlds. **Thursday** shares DNA with films like **Suicide Kings** (1997) and **Phoenix** (1998), examining how past sins poison attempts at normal life. Thomas Jane's performance as Casey Wells channels the desperate energy of Michael Madsen in **Reservoir Dogs** (1992), but with an everyman quality that grounds the escalating chaos.

The film's violence serves character development rather than mere shock value, similar to **A Simple Plan** (1998) and **U Turn** (1997). Each brutal encounter peels back layers of Casey's past while ratcheting up stakes. Aaron Eckhart's Dallas role previews his later work in **The Dark Knight** (2008), showing his talent for charming menace. SUBHEAD: Impact on Crime Cinema

sections.content: **Thursday** influenced later single-day crime thrillers like **Running Scared** (2006) and **Lucky Number Slevin** (2006). Its mix of black comedy and ultraviolence established a template for films like **Smokin' Aces** (2006) and **Seven Psychopaths** (2012). The film's tight focus on personal redemption amid criminal chaos echoes through works like **London Boulevard** (2010).
